Messages from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting the main and supplementary estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1964, were presented by Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I would like to make a statement concerning these estimates. The main estimates being tabled today are those which were prepared last fall and which have been the basis for the

Tabling of Estimates
operations conducted under authority oi special Governor General's warrants during April and May of the current year.
The supplementary estimates (A) are also being tabled today and contain the customary adjustments of the main estimates. Total budgetary expenditures in the main and supplementary estimates for 1963-64, including amounts already authorized by continuing statutes and moneys parliament is being requested to appropriate, amount to $6,545,504,515.
Because of the need for carrying on the financing of government operations by special warrant for the last two months of 1962-63 it will be necessary to await the appearance of the final expenditure figures for that year in order to make detailed comparisons. The government intends to report to parliament the total estimates and supply picture for 1962-63, following a detailed review being made to determine items and amounts which should properly be charged to the accounts of that year.
The royal commission on government organization, the Glassco commission, made suggestions for improving the form in which the estimates are presented to the house. These are at present under review but no change has been made in the form in which the estimates for the current fiscal year are now being presented.
With the permission of the house I now request that there be included in Hansard two tables relating to the estimates. The first table compares the 1963-64 estimates with the total budgetary estimates for several preceding years. The second table indicates the changes in the main estimates for 1962-63 and 1963-64, broken down by administration and operation, capital and other costs.
Mr. Speaker, there are two ways of effecting economies in government expenditures. The first is by a detailed examination of each item of expenditure and the particulars of each establishment. The second is by a realistic reappraisal of policies and programs approved in the past and carried forward from year to year more or less automatically. The purpose of such a reappraisal would be to see if certain programs that may have been quite justified and useful when originally introduced should now be dropped, or reduced in scope, in favour of new programs of greater importance under the economic and social conditions prevailing today. Both these approaches are needed if a thorough control over government expenditures is to be exercised. It may be, however, that the second approach of reappraising existing programs will provide greater opportunities for

eliminating or reducing less necessary government expenditures than a long drawn out examination of details, which sometimes degenerates into mere penny pinching.
Treasury board is now examining the programs of each department with the assistance and co-operation of the ministers concerned. Of necessity this examination will take some months to complete. Any reductions in the 1963-64 estimates which may result from this further examination and review will be reflected in the appropriations the house is asked subsequently to authorize.
The government is also pressing forward with a review of the recommendations made by the Glassco commission. Those recommendations of the commission that may be expected to result in greater efficiency throughout the public service or in useful savings of expenditures will be implemented as quickly as possible.
Does the house give permission to the Minister of Finance to have printed in Hansard the explanatory notes and attached tables relating to the 1963-64 estimates?

Agreed.

Kings): Mr. Speaker, the statement which has just been given to the house by the Minister of Finance in connection with the tabling of these estimates is, of course, of interest to all hon. members. All I can say at the moment is that we have listened with interest to the minister's statement and will give proper consideration to the explanations he has given. I presume, however, that the estimates which are now put before hon. members are the final estimates of his government in so far as the financial year is concerned, and we will not expect these to be amended except as further expenditures are required.
I am very happy to see some reference finally made to the report of the Glassco commission-
Hear, hear.

-and the fact that the present government is considering dealing with some of the economies which were recommended by that commission. At the moment, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing one can say in this matter except that we have before us today

the estimates for the coming year. I am not sure what procedure is going to be adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite in dealing with the estimates for the preceding year which, due to their own obstruction, were never approved by parliament.

I assume that some legislation will be brought in to validate those estimates, otherwise I think we on this side of the house will have to take a very careful look at this matter to decide what procedure we are to adopt. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice arising out of a statement made in Washington by the under secretary of agriculture regarding the rising price of sugar. In that connection he points out that the speculative bubble in sugar will burst under the weight of plentiful supplies.
Since I asked a question the other day, has the minister had any opportunity to look into this matter, and is he able to give the house any information having regard to the fact that the amount of sugar on hand in Canada as of March 31 last was considerably more than a year ago? Also, what present steps are being taken in connection with sugar prices which are proving so detrimental to those in the lower income tax brackets?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ACTION TAKEN WITH RESPECT TO RISING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apparently it is not a question we have heard, but a statement by the right hon. gentleman arising out of a press release from Washington.
I should like to point out to him and to the house, as I intended to do and tried to do on a former occasion, that the Combines Investigation Act is quite clear as to the responsibilities of the director of investigation and research with regard to investigations. The act is clearly directed and aimed at preventing, first, combinations in restraint of trade, which require a conspiracy to be proven, and, second, the abuses of a monopoly situation. The act is not concerned with the level of prices as such but rather with the manner in which they are established. The manner in which sugar prices have risen indicates no contravention of the statute.
However, my hon. friend did raise a question the other day which I brought to the attention of the director, and he has given me the following information which I should like to give to the house. The director has reported to me that the situation in Canada is a direct reflection of world market conditions over which Canada has no control, and that any action taken under the Combines Investigation Act cannot be expected to correct the situation.
In the light of the situation I am, therefore, exploring with my colleagues whether there are any other measures than can be taken within the constitutional authority of the federal government to alleviate the situation.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, today, employment offices in the Gaspe peninsula can supply us with rather accurate statistics on conditions at this time because in order to receive unemployment assistance benefits, heads of families, and all adults, must first report for employment at the national employment service office in order to qualify for social service relief. In my riding, more than 1,500 heads of families, or other adults, benefited from that social service last winter.
Though some legislation was adopted in the past which favoured one area or one province less than others, it should not be held against the Conservative party or the Liberal party. The blame should rest with the representatives of those areas.
On April 8 last, the people of Quebec expressed their confidence in the government members, after having given them a formal warning in June 1962. The era of great speeches containing fine promises by statesmen during the last 20 years, will not be accepted in Quebec from now on, and more particularly in my constituency.
Action is what is needed, and as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, industry has not been established in the Gaspe peninsula because our governments did not bother to do any planning.
Thanks to the Liberal government in Quebec, the whole of the Gaspe peninsula will have plenty of power this fall.
It is now up to the federal government to grant some fiscal advantages to industries who would set up there and, jointly with provincial authorities, to give them adequate means of transport and communication.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette) stated on May 21 last, as can be seen on page 8 of the appendix to Hansard:
The whole Quebec electoral machine was at work and the Liberal members from Quebec are aware that all sorts of allowances, especially social allowances, were very generously distributed during the election campaign by the inspectors of colonization, the inspectors of all departments who paid amounts of $50, $60 and $75 to needy families in those ridings.
We have had examples of that from the Gaspe peninsula.
Mr. Speaker, in my riding, I lost some votes to the Social Credit because I spoke against the present system of unemployment assistance as distributed by our social services.

My first duty is, of course, to offer the traditional words of congratulation to the mover (Miss Jewett) and the seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address. I also wish to join those who have preceded me in congratulating the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker on their elevation to the high offices they now hold.
In commenting on the speech from the throne, I wish to be counted among those members of the house who hold that it is not given to any one party alone to devise useful legislation at all times. Obviously, useful legislation has been brought in by alternate governments from time to time over the years. Rather, I believe, each member has a duty to represent the will of the electorate which sent him here. Many of my colleagues on both sides of the house are widely experienced in world affairs, in business and in human relations. Some are dedicated to

objectives well beyond the limited goals of party power. We all belong to the world as it is today and must handle its affairs, whether in terms of imposing austerity or of increasing welfare services, making trade adjustments or providing for expensive defence measures; we must deal with all these matters not only with good intentions but on the basis of proven knowledge and experience.
Having said this, I must acknowledge that I consider some of the proposals raised in the speech from the throne to be very commendable. Many of them could have far reaching consequences depending, of course, on how they are implemented. That does not prevent me, however, from deploring the conspicuous lack of certain items which the Canadian people had come to expect as a result of oft-repeated election promises by the Liberal party. A very notable omission, and one which many Liberal supporters will find difficult to understand, is the fact that there is no early indication of an increase in old age pensions. We were told this would be done immediately-it would now appear that "immediately" is not part of the first 60 days of decision. Many of us are wondering what happened to the pledge to introduce a health plan. During the election campaign it was certainly listed high in the rating of priorities. Nor did we hear anything of the grand scholarship scheme in the speech from the throne.
Another shortcoming in the speech is the scant attention paid to agriculture. Coming from the prairies as I do, I cannot refrain from making the observation that the election results showed this section of the country, which has been called the bread basket of the nation, to be also politically the most perceptive. In addition to this being a well deserved tribute to the former prime minister, it is also a firm indication that the former minister of agriculture, Hon. Alvin Hamilton, rendered this country yeoman service in the discharge of his important office. There is no doubt that Manitoba voted for the return of the two cabinet ministers, the widely travelled former minister of northern affairs, Hon. Walter Dinsdale, together with the house leader and minister of veterans affairs and defence in the last parliament, Hon. Gordon Churchill. While all former cabinet ministers from the prairies were themselves re-elected, we certainly expected them to take their place again on the government side of the house. I have no doubt that in the next election several years hence this will be the case.
All prairie provinces, and Manitoba in particular, would have liked to see included some amendments to the Crop Insurance Act to make it possible for the provinces to ex-

Mr. Speaker, there are two matters of some urgency which have already been brought before the house in different ways, and I just want to make passing reference to them again. The first is the contentious question of the T.C.A. overhaul base. The Address-Mr. Mullally frightens me over the outcome of this is that hon. members opposite now show no apparent misgiving over what until last January had caused many searching questions when they sat on this side regarding effective emergency measures, the dread effects of fallout, the futility of the arms race, and so on. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) reversed his convictions on that issue on January 12, and thereafter there have been no expressed misgivings from the Liberal party over nuclear arms for Canada. We are now, in effect, in the nuclear club.
In his C.B.C. broadcast of May 3, 1963, Professor Arthur L. Phelps of Kingston had this to say over the nuclear issue:
If Canada had taken-
-in the election, he is referring to-
-any effective policy against the nuclear thing it would have initiated a chain reaction around the world. It would, I think, have made both the United States and Russia re-assess their respective attitudes. It could have broken the log jam. Everything would have been dumped with a new sort of thud into the lap of the U.N. The result would be an unfixing of fixed attitudes. It would have set free a new kind of thinking. Indeed, it would have changed the international weather like a fresh wind. In fact, it would have underlined the truth just dawning in concerned informed minds that against nuclear war there is no defence anywhere, any more for anybody.
The Canadian people had a chance to give direction to political thought in our nuclear weapons problem. A brief wild gesture in the right direction might have changed the course of history. Canadians almost made that gesture, but we did not. Eventually this question will spread beyond party thinking, for I am convinced that there is a core of Canadian opinion in favour of an anti-nuclear stand. I refer to the repeated representations constantly being made to us by individuals, organizations, universities, and so on, and many of these are from high-minded persons who have as their main goal the ennobling aim of world peace.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of taking up my full allotted time since I am certain that my constituents are anxious to see some of the promised legislation enacted. I will therefore conclude by admonishing hon. members on the government benches to bring on good legislative proposals, for we on this side, together with all Canadians, hold high expectations from this government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join, first of all, with hon. members who have already spoken in extending to you, sir, my congratulations on your appointment as chairman of committees of the whole house. May I, through you, extend to Mr. Speaker my congratulations on his appointment to his esteemed office. I am sure that it is the sincere wish of all of us that

his tenure of office will be both successful and of long duration. May I also extend to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) my congratulations on his appointment as deputy chairman of committees of the whole house.
It is a very distinct pleasure for me to extend my congratulations to my colleagues, the hon. members for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), for the brilliant manner in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to take this occasion to express my gratitude to my colleagues who, by their many courtesies, have made my initiation to parliament much more enjoyable and much more meaningful. (Translation):
And now, Mr. Speaker, because I have a hard time with my French pronunciation, I ask my French speaking colleagues to be patient and indulgent.
Although I have studied French long enough in school and at college to be able to read it, I have spoken French too seldom to be fluent in it.
I hereby resolve to do something about it without delay. To that end, I call on my French Canadian colleagues to help me.
Living in a district of the island where French is seldom heard, I never had the opportunity to train my vocal chords in the use of the soft and gentle accents of the French language.
I am sorry that, because of my shortcomings, I have to stop murdering this beautiful language and take refuge right away in my mother tongue.
(Text):
It is my very great honour, Mr. Speaker, to represent the constituency of Kings, Prince Edward Island, in this house. Its physical beauty and rural charm are, I am sure, comparable with the most magnificent scenes anywhere in Canada. Cradled in the blue waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the fertile red soil, the green rolling countryside and the magnificent beaches of Prince Edward Island offer both native islander and visitor a landscape that is beautiful and an atmosphere that is relaxing. While we extol with justifiable pride the great natural beauties of our island, it is our island people that we most admire. I believe that the people I have the honour to represent are among the most sincere, the most generous, the most hospitable and the most independent people in Canada.
At this time, through you, Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend to them my sincere thanks for the great honour they have accorded me. and at the same time compliment them on
[Mr. Enns.l

their wisdom and foresight in electing a Liberal member. In this way they have made their contribution to the establishment of a Liberal government, a government that is destined to do great things for Canada and for the Canadian people, and at the same time make an outstanding contribution to the betterment of world conditions. I want to assure my constituents that I will always be mindful of my obligations to them, and that I will work at all times for those measures which will be of benefit to those whom I represent. May I also assure my honourable island friends opposite that the interests of my constituents will be in very capable hands, for many years to come.
While the rules of debate allow us to speak on a wide range of subjects during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I believe it is more in keeping with the spirit of the address, if not the letter, to confine one's remarks to a consideration of those matters which have been presented in the speech by His Excellency the Administrator, since this is an outline of the legislation the government proposes to present to parliament during this session. Therefore I shall discuss briefly various aspects of the speech dealing with trade, agriculture and fisheries, especially in their application to the area I represent and the Atlantic region in general. Of course, Mr. Speaker, in doing this we are very mindful that as members of parliament we must be concerned with national matters, while at the same time paying particular attention to the area we represent; because we cannot have a vigorous economy in the Atlantic provinces, for example, if the rest of the country is experiencing an economic recession. However, as legislation comes before parliament we will have an opportunity to discuss it both in its national and regional character.
In the Atlantic provinces our natural continental trading lines are north and south while the cherished political threads that bind Prince Edward Island to the rest of Canada run east and west. This has presented, and continues to present, one of the most serious obstacles to economic development and advancement in the Atlantic area. For this reason we are very concerned, probably more so than Canadians in other parts of the country, with all matters affecting trade. It is, therefore, a source of encouragement to us to learn from the speech from the throne that our far-seeing Liberal government believes that economic progress can best be achieved by steadily reducing the barriers limiting trade, and by taking those measures which are designed to expand Canada's export trade.
The Address-Mr. Mullally
The geographically natural trading routes for the Atlantic provinces lead us to the eastern seaboard of the United States, the Caribbean area and, indeed, in the broadest view to the entire European Atlantic community. I believe, therefore, that more efforts should be made, first of all, to establish a greater volume of trade between the Atlantic provinces and the West Indies and other areas in the Caribbean. Besides providing a new market for our products this would enable us to make use of carriage of goods by water, a very decisive factor at this time especially when rail freight is so prohibitively expensive, and rail service in general is being curtailed in eastern Canada.
Transportation is a great problem for us on Prince Edward Island because of the great distances that separate island producers from the markets of the rest of Canada. If proper investigation of these new markets and an easing of tariff restrictions could be arranged, then we would have a market closer at hand for our farm and fishery products, a market in the Caribbean and along the eastern seaboard of the United States which could efficiently and profitably be accommodated by water transport. We must therefore continually strive to seek ways and means to compensate for the difficulties under which we in the Atlantic provinces, in general, and we islanders, in particular, labour because of geographic and political exigencies.
Our government's program for agriculture as outlined in the speech from the throne will, I feel confident, appeal to the farmers in my constituency because it gives evidence of the government's concern for farmers everywhere. The provision of two ministers of agriculture should benefit farmers everywhere, in all parts of the country because, as the speech from the throne so clearly states, agriculture in both the Atlantic provinces and on the prairies will receive closer and more expert attention. This, of course, is quite understandable when the burden of this portfolio is, with forethought, divided in this manner. It is also very pleasing to read these words in the speech from the throne as found on page 7 of Hansard:
My ministers will institute new programs to make farming as a whole more stable and more prosperous.
We are faced with serious agricultural problems in my constituency which I am sure are not peculiar to this area alone. The relatively small size of our farms, the extremely high cost of machinery, the shortage of investment capital, the difficulties of transportation and the lack of an over-all well managed marketing program are only a few of the difficulties with which island farmers courageously do battle daily. Nearly 70 per

The Address-Mr. Mullally cent of the farms on the island are under 100 acres and with the high costs of present-day mechanized farm equipment the unit cost of production has become much too high in relation to the selling value of farm products, for island farmers to constitute effective competition. In the last decade, for example, the number of farm tractors on the island has increased by 75 per cent but at the same time the number of farms in operation has decreased by 30 per cent while the size of the farm unit has remained about constant. This means that overhead costs have risen to such a point that some measures must soon be taken to remedy the situation if economic tragedy for island farmers is to be averted.
As a rural islander, representing a rural constituency on Prince Edward Island, I would urge that some means be adopted to provide capital to enable island farmers to expand their land holdings. Land on the island is available but the capital necessary to exploit its productivity to the greatest financial advantage is not. The Farm Credit Corporation does not render our island farmers the longed-for assistance that we believed and hoped it would. The almost universal view with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation, which has so very often been expressed to me by island farmers, is that "we just got enough money from it to get into real trouble". We islanders believe that something should be done to make this federal agency a more effective vehicle of prosperity for island farmers.
Further, the cost of machinery for the small farm units presents a major obstacle to progress. As a feasible solution I exhort the executive to give immediate and serious consideration to the establishment of machinery banks by the federal government from which banks farm machinery could be rented by island farmers at a reasonable rate. In this way a machine could serve many farmers and its use would drastically reduce both the capital cost and the maintenance cost of the machinery.
Next, we require much more extensive research into practically every phase of the farm problem, especially into new crops, land use, methods of production and processing as well as the most economically effective methods of marketing. Much has been said, but little has been done on the island under ARDA, and its application, especially in relation to agriculture, has not, as island farmers see it, been clearly defined. It is quite conceivable that research, particularly in the nature of those things I have just mentioned, could be carried out as a project under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act.
Agriculture has undergone striking changes in our province, and if this industry is to survive and prosper we must propose and adopt new and imaginative measures, because this is the basic and most important industry on the island.
I was born and raised on an island farm. I know the farmers' problems and the difficulties under which they are labouring at this time. It is, therefore, with a knowledge gained from experience that I speak on their behalf.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I propose three measures which I believe will do much to improve the serious difficulties that our island farmers are facing at this time. First, I urge that easier credit terms and a more generous amount of investment capital be made available by the federal government to enable island farmers to expand their land holdings and extend their farm operations. Second, I propose the establishment of machinery banks by the federal government to help overcome the almost insurmountable difficulties in this field. Third, I propose the development of a program of research, financed by the federal government, into all aspects of island agriculture.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I direct the attention of this house to our second basic industry, one which is of great concern to all of us in the Atlantic region, the fishing industry. We have been making very little progress for several years in this country in the development of the fishing industry. This is especially apparent when we compare our fishery development with the rapid progress other countries have been making in recent times. It is, therefore, Mr. Speaker, more than encouraging to know that our Liberal government has expressed its intention to launch, in consultation with the provinces, a program of national fisheries development. It is the sincere hope of all islanders, of the people I represent, and I am sure of all the Atlantic provinces generally, that this will be a truly national program, a program broad in its application and designed to restore this once great Canadian industry to its rightful place in our national economy. There is a great opportunity and a great need for farsighted and realistic action by our Liberal government to expand and develop this second basic resource industry of Prince Edward Island.
It is with justifiable pride, Mr. Speaker, that I notify this house that we in Kings county, Prince Edward Island, who are fishermen and who are associated with the fishing industry, are enthusiastic in our support of the Prime Minister's sustained efforts to establish a 12-mile limit for our coastal fisheries. The intention to secure the establishment of a 12-mile limit for the use of Canadian

fishermen, as stated in the speech from the throne, has received the enthusiastic approval of my constituents. It has been welcomed by them as one of those bold, imaginative steps by a Liberal government to protect their cherished rights. If Canada is to protect its great marine resources for present and future Canadians, it is imperative that our government take the necessary steps as quickly as possible to stop the depletion of our productive fishing grounds which is being caused by the incursion of modern fishing craft from other countries. After our government has negotiated satisfactory arrangements respecting our recognized historic fishing rights with the United States and France, then a unilateral declaration can be made to prevent foreign fishing fleets from exploiting our Canadian fishing resources.
I was closely associated with the fishing industry for several years. I am well aware of the problems and the thinking of our fishermen. I can say emphatically that this is one measure which they have sought for many years, and for which they will thank this Liberal government in the future.
There are many other items of legislation about which I should have liked to speak. However, since this is my first speech before this distinguished assembly. I thought I should deal with those matters which are of immediate concern to my people, the farmers and fishermen of Prince Edward Island. I am sure that there will be occasions, as the session progresses, to deal with other matters of concern.
I have some ideas about procedure, the rules and general matters affecting our functions as representatives of our constituencies, and as members of this house. However, after less than two weeks in this house I feel that it would be premature for me to assume a dogmatic attitude concerning the best methods to adopt for the successful and expeditious dispatch of the nation's business.

speechtext:
When one feels such an air of concentrated excitement, upon rising before this mass audience, and contemplates the thousands of Hansards that are going to be sent out and to become thumb-worn, as one's speech is gone over, it certainly makes him feel that he is making a great impact upon the Canadian people. Dispensing with the irony for a minute, I should like to extend congratulations to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai), the congratulations of the entire lakehead region, upon his appointment as a parliamentary secretary. We are expecting a great deal from him and from the three cabinet ministers in the government representing northern Ontario. I do not know of a time in Canadian history when such an area, in
The Address-Mr. Fisher terms of population and in terms of such a natural geographic unit, had such powerful representation as in the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson).
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the horizon that is in front of northern Ontario, as it contemplates the light that is flashing from these three cabinet beacons, is almost more than we can face. However, we are going to hope that all this power will be reflected in consideration of some of the problems we have, particularly in relation to mining, forestry, transportation, secondary industry and such things.
One of the points I noted during the Prime Minister's speech in the throne speech debate was his reference to the former prime minister's passionate preoccupation with personalities. While he did not say so, he implied that this was wrong, that the former prime minister had not learned anything from his experience. Well, the main burden of my remarks will be directed towards the election and its aftermath. I want to talk largely in terms of personalities, because it is my feeling that concentration on personalities does not cloak the realities of the day: personalities express them. It is for this reason I preface my remarks with no apology for dealing largely with personalities. Moreover, I do insist that this is perhaps the most important avenue down which to look at politics today.
If one were to sum up the election very briefly he could say that none of the four parties that actually contested the election came off very well. I know the Liberals take a great deal of satisfaction out of forming the government. However, any cold blooded analysis of the situation would show their relative failure was the greatest. I recall encountering a certain cabinet minister, whom I shall not name, just a few weeks before the election. He was talking in terms of 160 or 170 seats. There was a sort of gay abandon in his air. The concrete result achieved on April 8 certainly set that optimism in a different kind of focus.
As individual members of parliament in this house, we are all successful, of course, and that is good for us. However, our parties, and our party-I make that distinction-all failed in a national way. Not one of the parties can take any tremendous amount of satisfaction from the last election.
I want to dig into some of the reasons why we have this rather unpromising and unflattering position of the parties at the present time. I want to start particularly in terms of

The Address-Mr. Fisher the personalities and in terms of the institutions, such as parliament, and the party machines and party programs. My analysis is made, having before me several glaring points regarding the present political situation-glaring and obvious to me and 1 imagine to all other hon. members here.
The first is that we need several years, certainly at least 18 months, without a federal election in this country. I think we need that space for simple reasons, reasons of equity such as the redistribution problem and the fact that we should not go back to the Canadian people again on a basis that will be 13 or 14 years out of date. I think we need that space in terms of continuity of budgeting and taxation; in terms of some kind of stability of administration in the relationships between the cabinet and the actual administrators, and the relationship between the cabinet, the administrators and the House of Commons.
We need the absence of an election, for 18 months to two years, because all the parties need to reorganize their party positions and party platforms, and of course while they will be doing this in the House of Commons in terms of the programs and attitudes they develop, I certainly speak for my own party when I say we realize how much of this has to be done outside. I am not thinking particularly in terms of party organization but in terms of our own provision for the Canadian people in the future with sharper, more clear-cut policies supported by some kind of study in depth, and of detailed reasons why we think the Canadian people should accept them.
The second glaring factor that seems to me to support the absence of an election is the fact that party leaderships are in such an indecisive position. Later on I shall refer to some of the Gallup poll analyses on this particular matter, but I do not think this point needs to be emphasized. It is quite apparent if one looks at the party situations, particularly the major party situations. Their leadership problems are substantial and they certainly need time to be worked out.
The last point in support of co-operation on our part to see that there is not an election is perhaps a Machiavellian one, a mysterious one, but it is simply this, that at present, there is a general scepticism and even intolerance on the part of the public with politicians and political parties. Maybe I overdraw that point, but I certainly sense it and encounter it in the correspondence I get as both a politician and as someone doing a bit of newspaper practice. Despite our own party contacts who will tend to put up with us willy-nilly, there is an over-all feeling


in the country that we have let the people down and are responding with the negative kind of performance they experienced in the last parliament. Therefore the best thing we can do as politicians is to give them some time, not so much to forget but, if one wishes to use a sociological word, for us to reorientate ourselves.
If one looks at what the election revealed in terms of party support he will find some very amazing things. I am one who has never believed, with regard to the final outcome on election night, that the Gallup poll is a completely accurate forecast, but I do know from personal observation of its use in the United States, and particularly in England, it gets onto opinions that are pretty sharply held by the Canadian people.
I have their release for May 4, which is headed "Community size; religion had sharp effect on vote." It goes on to say that the Roman Catholic vote was strong for the Liberals, being 59 per cent of their total in English Canada shown. I had this put to me in very amusing terms in one town in my constituency. When one of my supporters was on the church steps going into mass she encountered the Liberal organizer who said to her, "Look, Eva, you are the only person in the parish not voting Liberal this time. How about it?" I mention that as an example of something those of us who are in politics in English speaking Canada are aware of, and the Gallup confirms that core of strength. The Meisel studies done earlier revealed this for previous elections. The core of strength in the Liberal party during the last election and for some years, if you want to put it that way, was in the Roman Catholic vote.
I want to analyse something else this same survey put forward. Actually I do not want to analyse it; I want to give it as a fact, that in centres of over 100,000 population the Liberals had a much greater response and got much more support than the Conservative party, but as one went down to the smaller towns in rural areas the Conservative vote went up and the Liberal vote went down.
There is one other item that the Canadian Gallup poll came forward with, and the heading is this, "Liberal, not Conservative, was party of higher income." At first it struck me there was some kind of clash here. If the Liberal party was the party of higher income, and if the Liberal party was the party that had the Catholic vote and if, as all of these later papers show, the best educated people in the country tended to vote Liberal, then you had a very peculiar combination indeed.
On looking at this I finally came to the conclusion that the poll is correct. These are the three sources of strength which the

Liberal party had in the last election. Here was their greatest strength based on the tendency in English speaking Canada, and this is all this analysis will help me to work out. The Liberals got their greatest strength from the Roman Catholic vote, over 50 per cent in real figures of the vote of people with university education, and they also came up with the vote in the major cities.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you accept this as the basis of the strength of the party now in government and I, from my own experience feel this is so, you immediately begin to think of what this support means in terms of that party and what it will do. I happen to be one of those who, from observation, share the opinions expressed by Robert Fulford who recently did a biographical article in Maclean's magazine on the Prime Minister, in which he said as a politician the Prime Minister is almost completely eclectic, that he has an open mind and no set position, and that he takes things, or ideas as they come. If this analysis of the Prime Minister's personality is correct, then it is particularly important to know something about what the Liberal party may tend to do in view of the kind of support it has.
One of the election manifestations, and the Gallup poll does not show it, was that the communications industry was overwhelmingly in support of the Liberal party and the Prime Minister. It seems to me most of the people I know in the newspaper field were wearing Pearson hearts on their sleeves when working over their typewriters, and the same thing applied to the sound and television industry. I would sure like to have found somebody other than a Liberal working in the C.B.C. news and public affairs departments. If that may seem unfair I would like to point out it was unfair to all the other parties.
If anyone wants to get social-scientific on this, down at M.I.T. they made some studies which show that despite any objectivity a reporter wants to have, his application is conditioned by his basic bias, and it certainly was apparent the basic bias of the people doing reporting and commentating, in the newspaper field in particular, had swung first in complete antagonism to the former prime minister and second, in support of the Liberal party.
If any Liberals listening feel that this is a position devoutly to be maintained, I would like to point out to them that those same people are somewhat mercurial. If they will go back to 1958 they may remember that the hearts and the slaves were not red hearts but blue, and they were pulling for the then prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker.
The other basis of Liberal support that is quite apparent-one of the hon. members
The Address-Mr. Fisher from Alberta mentioned it and I certainly encountered it in my area-is that of the large corporations, who were out and out in support of the Liberal party not only with the funds they put up but also in the kind of administrative support they could give. When I say this, I am not complaining. As a matter of fact, if you look at it rightly you can turn this to your advantage. It is possible to do this. There are certain people who do become suspicious when they discover that one political party has the support of the major corporations in this country. But I think this is important because it is this industrial group that in my experience as a member of parliament is the most effective pressure group which influences the kind of policy that a government is going to develop. There is one other group that I must congratulate the Liberal party for, in essence, getting away from their appeal. I always regretted, and I know other people with my approach have regretted it, the emphasis upon the so-called ethnic vote. I feel that one of the good things that has come out of the last two elections is that we are really going to stop thinking in terms of orienting toward the so-called ethnic groups.
The last group, and the one I feel is an important pressure group or idea group in the country, which the polls term college vote people, although they do not have to be college vote people, are the intellectuals in the country, the brains. I do not know that as Canadians we can feel we have too many of these, because it is pretty obvious from immigration statistics that a good many of them disappear and have been disappearing over the years into the United States. But it is a fact that I encountered in my contacts with university people that the overwhelming majority of people in the academic and university fields and in the fields that are close to and have a relationship with, you may say, high culture, were supporting the Liberal party. This was largely as a very strong reaction; not so much because they were seized with the Liberal party and what it was offering, but because of a tremendously strong reaction to the former prime minister and the kind of "little folk, little men" presentation that he was giving. If you want to look at these things and then put your focus on the Liberal party and its leadership, its personalities and its direction, it seems to me you come up with the answer that, given this kind of support, you can have both hopes and fears about where this government may go.
Anyone who has read the debates is aware that you only have to read a paragraph from

The Address-Mr. Fisher the speech of the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and compare it with a paragraph from the speech of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) to realize that here are two young people in the party and there is a considerable divergence in their views. The question from our point of view is, which kind of path or direction is the Liberal party going to take? This is, as far as we are concerned, the most important of all questions. One of the things that has not been mentioned before but which certainly ties in with the election campaign is this. I hope the Liberal party will get off their imitation and organizational mocking of the Democratic party, and particularly the Kennedy image kind of thing. It seems to me that if they read some of the more acute United States periodicals they would realize that they have been criticizing all this "vigor" stuff and a lot of American people are beginning to realize that the Kennedy administration is really not the answer, that in Kennedy they have not got a Truman-I was going to say, they have not got a Roosevelt, but certainly they have not got even a Truman in terms of real drive and accomplishment. In this regard there is on the American scene more image than content. I feel that the reversals in imagery the Liberal party had in the last campaign should lead them to consider that this is one thing they should eschew.
We think a number of things are possible for this party in this parliament and we are looking at the Liberal government and hoping it will do certain things. My colleagues may not agree with this, but I have marked up what I might call the three positions, the Gordon position, the Sharp position and the Pickersgill position. If I might use United States personalities, I would compare the Pickersgill position to that of Senator Harry Byrd, the Gordon position to that of Hubert Humphries and the Sharp position to that of Mr. McNamara, the United States secretary of defence. I am thinking more of attitudes of personalities rather than position. If we look at the Byrd position, or the Pickersgill position, this is really the attitude that the Liberal party can handle things very well by divine right. In their minds they have the ability to straighten out the country and keep it going. This I mention first because it is the aspect of the Liberal party about which we have the least hope, because I think this ability is questionable. We will be watching very closely for the emergence in domination in the party of the divine right concept. We have very little hope for that and we think it could tend to merge into what I call the Sharp position, or, in paradox terms, the


McNamara position, that is the administrator of some genius and moderation.
This, it seems to me, in the short run may be very fine, but if we are going to meet the economic problems that our party sees Canada facing and needing solutions for, we will have to have a more radical influence in charge within the Liberal party. Mind you, I have mentioned the fact that I do not think the Prime Minister-I do not want to phrase this in terms that he has not got any ideas in his head, because it is not really that, but he is the kind of person who will seize upon ideas that are beamed to his head and will give them, I hope, some leadership. What I am suggesting is that the direction we want the Liberal party to follow is one in which there will be radical and progressive ideas, ideas which show an increasing urgency on the part of the government to give leadership and accept responsibility in economic matters. This will determine our support, our appreciation and probably our antagonism, if that should become necessary, to the Liberal party. We want to watch very closely and distinguish the influence of the various pressure groups that I have mentioned earlier.
Something that is most encouraging to me is the fact that in the core support that the Liberal party has with the Roman Catholics in English speaking Canada there is a spirit abroad today in the Catholic church which is certainly excited and stimulated by the two great encyclicals of Pope John; these look at political matters and at the form of government organization and its relationships with the people in a most advanced and radical way. During the election campaign I used to read out parts of the encyclical "mater et magistra" and I would ask the audience where they thought they came from. It was surprising how often they thought they came from the New Democratic party platform.
We are looking for many things from the Liberal party and will be showing an intense interest in their personalities and what is revealed. We are going to be sensitive, to undertake quite a critical exegesis with regard to all their statements. For instance, we want to know how much influence Mr. Lamontagne is going to have. I give his name in the clear because it is important in the terms of what he stood for before he came into the cabinet. We do not want to get into joshing about the role of the great Tom Kent, but I think here again we will be watching to see what happens. Some of us at least will be hopeful that the kind of promises that Mr. Kent could make as a politician will appear in the program that is put before us.

One of the things I enjoyed most on the day the throne speech was put before us was the appearance of the former minister of agriculture on television, where he told us three times that this throne speech perpetuated a fraud. I felt this was a real dandy. I do not know quite where he figured the fraud started. I felt maybe he meant "perpetrated". But if he felt there was a fraud perpetuated I would have thought he would have nailed it down and pinpointed its beginning. Not unrelated to this, it occurs to me we had a former cabinet minister speak in this house yesterday; if the Liberals perpetuated a fraud at least he perpetuated one of the biggest switches we have seen. He came into this house and sounded like some mossback in political terms who had crawled in here from the early nineteenth century. The kind of opposition he was attempting was such a contrast to the general imaginative and visionary line-I am not being nasty about this-that the Diefenbaker government took at times; so different that it does not make sense to me. If this is the kind of opposition the Conservative party is going to turn to in its philosophical terms we welcome it as a political party but we wonder, frankly, where it is going to lead them.
Some people are going to ask: what about the attitude of your own party? I repeat again, as I said earlier, our party needs a more clearcut philosophy. We need to do more planning in depth about our own program as well as talking in general terms, as I know we do, about the beneficence of economic planning.
I wanted to touch on some of the calls we are hearing now about the need for parliamentary reform, because this comes into the future picture. One of the things I noted about this debate is the nice way in which the cabinet has moved back and given the new people an opportunity to speak. This is good tactics and it bespeaks a generosity on their part which is truly great. I remember that when in opposition we used to talk about the four horsemen who hogged all the talk. Now they have got all kinds of horsemen in the corral and a few of us are wondering if we are ever going to see some of the lead horses again. They have certainly not been apparent in this debate.
This reflects one of the problems I have noted in this house and that is the distinction between the government backbencher and any other backbencher and also the distinction between the backbencher at any time of any party and what I call the so-called stars of the House of Commons, where we definitely have a star system. One of the reasons, it seems to me, why we never get anywhere
The Address-Mr. Fisher with proposals for reform is because traditionally this parliament has been in the hands of a cluster of what you might call stars. I was amused at hearing one of the new brighter members of the Liberal party feeding me the line given to him by his leaders that the thing to do is to come in here and take your time; there is no rush; it is a complicated place and you have got to get used to it. I trust he sits and takes his time until eternity, in political terms.
Our system does not allow any real purpose for a backbencher. His responsibility is to get elected on election night. Then he must be counted on to do so again at the next election. In the interim, he vegetates and looks after his sacred riding.
If we were serious in this talk about parliamentary reform we have to come to some decisions about what standards of performance should be expected of backbenchers. Should we have a roll-call here so that we might have some standard of attendance? Let us just not demand more or better parliamentary committees. How are we going to get better committees if we do not allow backbenchers more scope and opportunity in terms of research facilities? I hear people talk about the importance of research, but one of the things which has never been really settled is whether this research should be centred on the party organization or on the parliamentary library or whether it should be fed directly to the member himself. We have no standard of performance here and the traditional line seems to be the amateur gentleman line best symbolized by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) when he rose a few years ago in this house with beautiful unction and told us he hoped the day would never come when being a member of parliament was a full time job. There is what you might call the amateur gentleman conception of the member of parliament, and then there is the one that it is a full time job which requires and demands all one's energy and support in terms of money and research and then opportunities within the House of Commons itself to do something.
Frankly, it is possible for anyone who is pushing and has a lot of gall-and I am pushing and I would certainly not deny that I have gall-to operate within the confines of this institution and, to some degree, to achieve what I set out to achieve for my constituency and perhaps for my party. But if we are going to reform this system we have to make reforms which will affect all members including some of the more shy ones or the ones who perhaps need a great deal more encouragement than somebody like me.

The Address-Mr. Fisher
The idea that the Americans have where a senator or a congressman conducts himself like a Roman pro-consul who can roam the world with tremendous resources at his command and defy the party at any time is really the thing that tends to frighten our party leaders, particularly our major party leaders. They do not like to give such scope. When the former government was in control, one of the things I used to notice was that everybody was somewhat fearful that if they did allow such latitude someone would commit a gaffe. I remember when one young fellow went to Paris and said something which was not approved-and what a tearing down he got. This reflects this hesitation on the part of Canadian party leaders to give the support and the free rein which are enjoyed elsewhere.
I see you are about to rise, Mr. Speaker, and I should just like to thank the house for this magnificent audience. I shall look forward to going into greater detail on some future occasion regarding the matter of parliamentary reform.

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, may I first associate myself with the many other members who have congratulated you, sir, and the Speaker on your elections to the important posts you both now occupy?
I would also like to congratulate the mover (Miss Jewett) and seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and also the numerous other members who in speaking in this debate have made, as I am making, their first speeches in what is, to us, the strange atmosphere of this chamber. I assure them that if they were not nervous, I am.
It is a pleasure and a great honour to represent the constituency of Kindersley, one of the finest farming areas in the province of Saskatchewan. It not only has some of the finest grain land in the province but it also has some very fine pasture land. The combination of these two gives us a great diversification in farming. However, this constituency is not only fortunate in that respect but in others as well. We are fortunate in having oil, gas and salt located in my constituency, and founded on that base the industrialization of the constituency, I am sure, is only a matter of time.
It is a pleasure to me, too, to represent this constituency since the constituency has had the very great honour of having the former member for the constituency, Mr. R. L. Han-bidge, appointed as lieutenant governor for the province of Saskatchewan, a position which I am sure you will agree, as is evident from the applause, he will fill with distinction and charm.
Kindersley constituency, then, not only has some of the best wheat growing land, as well as some of the finest pasture land in the province, but because it has this industrial base it is growing very rapidly. I have in my constituency two of the fastest growing towns in the province of Saskatchewan. In common with much of this area Kindersley constituency suffers from the usual growing pains. Fifty years ago Kindersley constituency was nothing but wilderness with a few railway lines snaking across that wilderness. Settlement followed these lines, so that these railway lines are today an extremely important part of the lives of my people. Therefore, we are much concerned about the talk of railway line abandonment. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcll-raith) say that careful consideration was being given to this matter. May I respectfully suggest to him that if, and I repeat if, these railway line abandonments are to be proceeded with, then his government must find satisfactory means of enabling the farmer to send his crop to market. Not only must this

be done, but it must be done at fair prices for the alternative transportation services which will have to be provided.
We have one other problem which we hope the government can assist in solving. While only general indications have been given as to what type and kind of project the municipal development fund will assist, I would hope that it might provide funds to solve the matter of water shortage which a number of related communities in my constituency are presently greatly concerned with. Without water even the oil, gas and salt in my constituency is going to have a great deal of trouble in producing the industrial growth and expansion which I am sure would otherwise occur, but which will be limited by water shortage.
In general, the philosophic basis of the speech from the throne is easy to agree with. Its brevity is not necessarily a source of weakness. However, I am compelled to agree with my colleague the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that the attempt in the address to spell out cures does so by multiplying the bureaucratic agencies, of which I am convinced we have enough today. I am also quite convinced that the people of Canada do not have much faith in the ability of a bureaucracy to solve their problems. Instead they want their government, through this parliament, to take effective and specific measures to do so. There seems little evidence of these measures in the speech from the throne, and what there are in some instances would indicate that sober second thought is needed.
I would in particular refer to the decision to appoint two ministers of agriculture. Without question this is an unpopular move in the west. The farm organizations have said so in very explicit and definite terms. I need repeat only one argument which seems incontrovertible. Two ministers will be one other factor dividing the country into regional blocs. Yesterday morning the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) refused to state whether there would be two departments, one for each minister. If there is and each is to have a department of his own, we have a proliferation of bureaucracy with, in my opinion, no increase in efficiency. If there is to be only one department, conflict will be certain to occur between the two heads, the two ministers of agriculture. However, we would all be prepared to accept gratefully two ministers of agriculture if they can do as good a job for the farmers as the former minister of agriculture did during the last five years. They have facing them an extremely difficult problem if they are to sell our grain. Every wheat grower hopes that they are successful in continuing the China wheat sales. How-
The Address-Mr. Cantelon ever, if they do not do better for the farmer than this government has done in the new milk and milk products sales regulations, I am afraid that the wheat farmer is in for real trouble. The exposition of its weaknesses by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) was masterful and he is to be commended for it. Even though this government does not like advice it would do well to heed his.
If the government is to sell our grain it will have to realize, as the Liberal government of 1956 failed to do, and as the past Conservative government did realize that the day of the seller's market in grain is gone. The seller must take every possible step to push sales. The last government succeeded. This government has already given evidence of its closed mind arrogance when it replied to the good advice of the previous minister of agriculture, as reported on a television interview, that it did not need advice from the last minister of agriculture, although there is no one better qualified to give such advice. There has been born into this world only one man who did not need advice from other men. This know-it-all attitude of the government does not give much hope for success.
The announcement of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) made prior to the opening of the house, that the government intended to use $10 million to provide 10,000 scholarships to university students is something that every educator in the dominion should welcome. Certainly I do. However, this welcome gesture is only that. It does not begin to cope with the two main problems facing the universities today-lack of accommodation and shortage of teaching personnel. These two problems can be solved and they will be solved by the universities themselves if they are given the necessary funds. And where are the universities to get this money, if it is not mostly supplied from the federal treasury? Yesterday morning the Prime Minister stated that the matter of university aid would be considered in relation to other financial needs of the country. This does not sound too hopeful for the universities.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on record some estimates of just what that need will be in the next few years. These estimates were supplied by the Canadian Teachers' Federation. In the academic year 1962-63 it is estimated that full time student enrolment in the universities will be 137,000. In 1965-66 it is estimated the enrolment will be 182,900. The operating expenses too, will rise per student. In 1962-63 the operating expense per student will be $1,797. There will be a regular increase each year, so that in 1965-66 the cost will have risen to $2,094. This will mean total

The Address-Mr. Cantelon operating expenditures in the millions of dollars-$246 million in 1962-63 and $383 million in 1965-66. Thus the percentage increase each year over expenditures of the previous year will run from 15 to 17 per cent.
The estimate of the need with regard to teaching personnel indicates an equally serious situation. If one dips into the past for a year or two he finds that in 1955-56 there were 6,000 persons teaching in the universities, while in 1960-61 the number was 9,000, an increase of 50 per cent in five years. The projected need indicates that in 1965-66, there will be 14,000 required and in 1970-71, there will be 25,000.
I repeat that the universities themselves can solve these problems if they are given the money. Since people are any country's greatest resource, it is my contention that this assembly is morally bound to provide the university institutions with the necessary funds. The past government's method of making grants to the universities does not violate provincial rights since the federal parliament does not maintain any control over how the universities spend the moneys. These grants can be readily increased.
Not only are our universities in difficulties but our secondary schools also need comparable help. To see that the provinces receive this help without violating the principle of non-interference with their educational rights may be more difficult. But the old saying, where there is a will there is a way, is just as applicable today as it ever was. We should have that will. One way in which the past government provided help was by assisting in vocational education. In 1960 some $10,694,000 was provided to the provinces in this way. The statistics for the year 1961 have not been released but I believe a fair estimate would be something over $25 million. However, between April, 1961 and January 28, 1963 the federal share of co-operative projects in this field amounted to $292,800,000. This is worth-while aid. The present government should continue it. The poorest child in the poorest region of Canada is entitled to the best education this country can provide. We cannot afford to waste our human resources. I have only touched on this matter and I hope in the future to be able to expand upon it.
Some other members have expressed their beliefs as to their parties and what they think those parties stand for. I should like to conclude by stating what I think the Progressive Conservative party has demonstrated it stands for today. First, it stands for a united Canada. Second, it stands for equality of opportunity for all parts of Canada and equal rights for all peoples, races and religions in Canada. Third, it stands for Canada

for Canadians. So long as it continues to support these principles I shall be proud to represent Kindersley as a member of the Progressive Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to add my congratulations to those that have already been extended to the new Speaker and Deputy Speaker on their appointments. My constituency is one constituency removed from that of the Speaker, and I might tell the house that the Speaker has enjoyed the confidence of his constituents for many years. They are happy that this house now shares their sentiments and high regard for him. I also wish to add congratulations to the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) on having set a very high standard of debate in this house.
I should like to take a moment to pay tribute to my predecessor, Mr. Leon Crestohl, who passed away some three days prior to the close of nominations. I may tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I campaigned in the constituency of Cartier and he was held in extremely high regard by his constituents. His passing is a loss not only to the constituency of Cartier but to Canada as well.
(Translation):
I have the honour of representing in this house the constituency of Cartier which is situated in the heart of Montreal, since St. Lawrence boulevard, which is the dividing line between east and west, crosses it from north to south.
Cartier is probably the most cosmopolitan riding in Canada, as several languages are spoken there. Almost half of my constituents are French speaking and the other half includes almost all ethnic groups.
All ethnic groups hope that the great French culture and the great English culture in our country will, as soon as possible, progress on an equal basis.
(Text):
The ethnic groups of Canada, who recognize the position held in this country by the French speaking and English speaking cultures, want to remind Canada that there is still a third culture in this country which may be called the multiculture of the ethnic groups. The ethnic groups now compose 25 per cent of the population of this country. When we admit immigrants to this country we are for the most part admitting the cream of the people of the countries from which they come, because it takes great courage for a man to pull up his roots and to emigrate to a foreign country.

He does not understand the language and he must enter into competition with the people there. These are the kind of people we want in Canada because when they build for themselves they help to build Canada.
It is true that it is a privilege for an immigrant to be allowed to enter Canada but this is not a one-way street because the immigrant or, for want of a better word, the new Canadian adds and contributes to the country. I submit that the United States of America entered upon its greatness when it allowed waves of immigrants to come into that coun-depends in large part upon the successes of the laboratories and research departments such as are now being operated in the United States of America. I would venture to say that if it were not for the scientists of the ethnic groups there would have been no Manhattan project.
In 1933, Hitler came to power in Germany and by act of God or by act of providence, Franklin Delano Roosevelt became president of the United States. It was then that the struggle between good and evil commenced. It was at that time, Mr. Speaker, that the United States of America welcomed to its borders the great German scientist, Albert Einstein who, under the protective roof of Princeton University, brought forward the formula that gave birth to the atomic age. Then, an equally great refugee, a great Italian scientist, Enrico Fermi, who was a world Nobel prize winner in 1939 and who fled from fascism, established himself in the United States of America and set off in the University of Chicago in 1945 the first nuclear reaction. These two great refugees, these two neo-Americans, both came from a race that knew the meaning of persecution.
It is a fortunate thing, Mr. Speaker, that these two scientists found their way to the United States. Had they remained in their lands of origin, it is possible that the atomic age might have belonged to Hitler or, perhaps to Stalin. If that had been the case, instead of Nagasaki and Hiroshima, it might have been London, Paris, New York or Montreal.
I am somewhat dismayed by some of the speeches I have heard which practically deprecated the existence of the United States of America. If we are to count our blessings, surely one of those blessings is the fact we are located geographically north of the United States of America instead of geographically north of the Soviet union. Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania once existed north of the Soviet union, but they no longer exist. We have been saying to Europe for more than a century: why can't you live in Europe the
The Address

Mr. Klein way we live here in America? We live beside the United States of America. We have a common border of 3,000 miles, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. There are no troops, no guns and no planes. To whom does the credit go, to us with 18 million people or to them with 180 million people? If the people of Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia could speak to us today, they would tell us how fortunate we are that we are living next door to the greatest, the finest, most powerful democracy in the world.
Some of us have been saying, in effect: Yankee, go home. Some of us have gone beyond the South American countries and have said, "Yankee go home, and take your Yankee dollar with you." They have said, "We do not want your magazines; we do not want your nuclear warheads; we do not want any part of your culture. We want very little of you, but for God's sake if we are attacked you must come and defend us." Prior to April 8, we were not popular in England. We were not popular in the United States. It would seem to me that the only places where we might have won a popularity contest were in Cuba or red China.
I say it is a great commentary, Mr. Speaker, upon the greatness of the democracy to the south of us that we can say whatever we want against the United States without fear of oppressive retaliation. Hungary had freedom for three days. The people spoke out against the Soviet union and the red tanks rolled back into Budapest. In 1945, when the war ended the United States possessed the most destructive weapon that has ever been possessed in the world. She had in her hands the power to possess any country that she wanted. She could have threatened the sovereignty of any country she wanted. She did not take one foot of soil belonging to any other country and did not touch one inch of sovereignty belonging to any other nation on this globe. This is the kind of nation we have to the south of us.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that is indisputable, that if any nation in the western world has sovereignty today, if England has sovereignty, if France has sovereignty, and even if Canada has sovereignty today, it is due to the great nuclear deterrent power of the United States of America.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that Canada should go forward in partnership with the United States, not as a satellite but as a partner, in this great North American adventure. God bless Canada, but God bless America too.

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
