speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate is in its final few minutes and I do not want to be the one to bring to a conclusion a discussion that has ranged over a very wide area of interests, domestic as well as external. The good book says that the last shall be first and the first shall be last. I should like to extend congratulations, for a very special reason, to the mover (Miss Jewett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. She represents a professional group in Canada that has appeared only recently in governmental circles at the national level. I refer, of course, to the members of the teaching profession, and particularly professional political scientists. I should like to extend congratulations to her on the quality of her presentation and also because she has given the lie to that old saw which is said to apply to those in the teaching profession, to the effect that those who can, do and those who cannot, teach. I think that her accession to this house is a very worthwhile innovation indeed.
I should like to extend my congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker. I want to take this opportunity to return a compliment that you extended to me and about which you have no doubt forgotten. When I first came to this house back in 1951, you were one of the first members to invite me to the parliamentary restaurant to give me a fatherly talk on the duties and responsibilities of members in this chamber. Those are little courtesies that one does not forget in the hurly-burly of parliamentary life. I must admit I did not take all of your advice on that occasion, but as you sit in the chair presiding over the deliberations of this house and holding in your custody the rights and privileges of all hon. members, I am sure I can agree with everyone else who has spoken along these lines, that you will discharge your responsibilities with the distinction you have shown in all the duties you have undertaken in the house.
Mr. Speaker, it has become obvious during this debate that one of the prime slogans of the new government, incidentally a slogan that was imported from abroad, "let's get the economy moving again," was a rather unfortunate one from the standpoint of the new government. I think it has become evident, in the course of the many speeches already made, that the economy was moving much faster and more programs were proceeding than the members of the new administration had realized, or at least had cared to admit.
I think the slogan was chosen because they had become bamboozled by their own propaganda which, time out of number, came out


with slogans such as "The economy of Canada is sick," "We are confronted with runaway inflation," and that the former administration was stumbling and bumbling, or words to that effect. The stumbling and bumbling in the next few weeks will not apply to the administration that has just departed but to the new administration that has come in. I say that with modesty, because I realize there are tremendous problems confronting Canada, and any hon. member, whether he be a member of the government or not, has to recognize he is subject to all human foibles and there is no elixir of life, no universal solvent, that is going to resolve all the problems confronting Canada at present.
I am sure that very often in their quieter moments of meditation the new ministers- to paraphrase the title of one Broadway production that has been running for some time-have wished "Stop the world, I want to get off." I am sure some of them have had that same reaction to the rapid events and to the policies and programs they have taken over and for which they are now responsible.
So far as I can see, looking at the throne speech, the policies enunciated by the government thus far are either a continuation or an enlargement of programs and policies that were under way. In fact, if you look at it mathematically you find that the pieces of government legislation on the order paper to date number eight, whereas for the same period of the last parliamentary session there were 21 pieces of government legislation before the House of Commons. Yet these distinguished gentlemen who now occupy the treasury benches went about the country, either deliberately or deluded by their own propaganda techniques, telling the people of Canada that the former administration was a government of inaction without progress, without policy, without purpose.
I have been trying to imagine what might have persuaded the new administration to adopt this slogan "Let's get the economy going again," which resulted in the inevitable corollary

the famous 60 days of action. I believe such slogans resulted from a deep seated sense of guilt which has carried over from the period when members of the Liberal party last occupied the treasury benches. I quote as my authority in that respect none other than the leader of that party, the present Prime Minister, in the famous conclusion whereby he summed up the defeat of the government in 1957 when he said, in his typical choice of phraseology, the brass had got out of touch with the grass. The years of neglect, indifference and complacency had caught up with the previous administration, and returning to power on the waves of propaganda which largely constituted the last

election campaign, and now burdened with a sense of guilt for the lack of activity during their previous 22 years in office, they decided to try to make up for lost time, but there is an old saw which says more haste less speed. I am sure it has already been demonstrated to them that this is true.
We talk about the need of adjusting to the tremendous changes facing Canada and the world at the present time, but I would suggest that the time when Canada should have been adjusting to those changes was in the years immediately following world war II, and no amount of frenzied activity not connected with thought and planning is going to make up for the years that the locusts have eaten.
I have only time to deal with three areas which demonstrate that in this so-called program of getting the economy going again, this 60 days of decision, lack of careful foresight and planning is already evident. I shall deal first with the field of agriculture. It was obvious in the late forties and early fifties that our agricultural industry was faced with major problems, but the only answer we could get from the government of that day was that the farmers never had it so good, that all would be for the best in the best of all possible worlds. It was obvious then that there was a rural-urban drift under way, and this has now been recognized on all sides. The farmers were leaving their rural environment and moving to the new metropolitan communities. This now constitutes one of our major social problems, but nothing was done to assist in the adjustment to this fundamental process of social change. Mechanization was under way. The cost-price squeeze was one of the main reasons behind the rural-urban drift, but no action was taken to deal with it. There was educational rigidity and educational inadequacy, particularly in the rural communities.
The Liberal party talk about a government stumbling and fumbling, but in six years of Conservative administration the major problems that beset the agricultural community -and the well being of that community is basic to the national well being-were dealt with and the results are already evident. I do not have to go through the programs and the policies. The support of the rural communities is indicative of their endorsation of the programs that were speedily carried out. I know there is a tendency on the part of the pundits as well as the politicians to say that we now have a voting dichotomy in Canada between the rural and the urban community. But it is not a clearcut distinction of that kind. It is, rather, that the areas which were
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale more susceptible to the propaganda techniques of the Liberal party reluctantly moved in that direction in sufficiently large numbers to give a moderate majority. But in the areas where programs of national development really count, where there were real problems of social adjustment, the voters of Canada soundly endorsed the policies of the former administration.
I should just like to refer to the ARDA program, the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. This is a major piece of legislation, arising out of the resources for tomorrow conference, which is going to transform the face of rural Canada as well as urban Canada in the next few years. It should have been undertaken at least a decade before it actually was dealt with. However, as I have already indicated, the immediate post-war years were marked with neglect, indifference and complacency. ARDA is just as broad as the people of Canada wish it to be. The most important aspect of ARDA is that it places the initiative in the hands of the local communities. No bureaucracy from the top can control the operations of ARDA. The program provides the legislative framework for local initiative to deal with local problems, alternative uses for land, new industrial activity in the transformation taking place in the rural communities, and retraining for the people who have been displaced in the great rural-urban drift that has been taking place during recent years.
What do we have substituted for this vigorous, visionary program? We have a plan to introduce two agricultural ministers in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I would say this is merely a political gimmick and will solve nothing. In fact it will only aggravate and intensify the problem, because agricultural matters in Canada, as is the case in other economic spheres, are indivisible; you cannot segregate or separate Canada into east and west in this regard.
Then I would refer to some of the statements made with regard to solving the wheat problem, the $2 a bushel wheat for example. I would point out that as the new government proceeds to implement this policy-and it is duty bound to do so because this was a solemn promise made during the election- they are going to wreak havoc in one of the major problem areas of the farming community in Canada; that is, to the preservation of the family farm. Their policy will have this effect because $2 a bushel wheat will give maximum support to the large farmer and minimum support to the smaller farmer, who is feeling the pressure of the cost-price squeeze at the moment. I say, Mr. Speaker, that a prosperous agricultural industry and a thriving agricultural community is still

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale basic to the welfare and the well being of Canada. The fact that this important sector of the economy was completely omitted from the speech from the throne is an indication of the new government's dereliction in this regard. I am sure that a good deal of the present economic upsurge can be traced to the increased purchasing power that has been made available by the successful agricultural program of the Conservative administration.
Mr. Speaker, there was no reference at all to the field of education in the speech from the throne. I would point out that we have had a crisis in education ever since the 1930's, and certainly since the end of world war II. Everybody used to talk about it and nobody did anything about it. When I first came into this house in 1951 it was impossible to have the subject even discussed intelligently because of the buck-passing technique, the logrolling technique between the constitutional authority of Ottawa and the authority of the provinces which was resorted to by the former Liberal administration. They said this was a subject under the purview of the provinces and there was therefore no responsibility at the Ottawa level. The former administration moved vigorously in this field. We instituted the vocational and technical training program, grants to universities doubled, we gave construction assistance to institutions housing the important faculties of the humanities and social sciences. These have all been a long step forward. In the face of the presentation made by the representatives of the Canadian university foundation just the other day I would quote from the Gordon commission report to remind the new administration that if they are going to take vigorous and visionary action they must do something constructive and positive in this area of education. In other words they must follow up the programs already initiated by the former Conservative administration. I quote from the Gordon commission report:
It is our duty ... to point out most emphatically that it is vitally important to Canada's future for the status of our universities to be improved and strengthened, and for their facilities to be increased ... In this connection it must suffice us to express the strong opinion that no government which bears any share of responsibility for the future economic development of this country can allow a solution to the pressing financial problems of the universities to go by default.
I would remind the new government, and particularly its Minister of Finance, of their responsibilities in this respect. During the recent election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) visited my constituency. I regret to say that he was not extended the hospitality for which western Canada is noted.

speechtext:
Shame.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I had nothing to do with it. In order to get into the mood of the occasion I wore a lovely, red trapper's coat just to show that everything was impartial and on a very high level. But the Prime Minister made the unfortunate mistake of holding his reception in the new building in Brandon College which had been provided by the forward looking educational assistance programs of the Conservative administration. He was there making promises about federal aid to education, about university scholarships and about all sorts of wonderful things that were going to happen in the field of education. I wish there had been some reference to this in the speech from the throne. Mr. Speaker, Brandon College, like other institutions of higher learning, languished for many years following world war II. That building in the city of Brandon in which the Prime Minister spoke was the first to be built under the construction grants program that had been made possible by the former administration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is not what the college told me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I personally had the privilege, Mr. Speaker, of turning the sod. I must bring my remarks to a conclusion. Right across the board, right across the whole gamut of educational activity in Manitoba there has been a wonderful transformation. This has been made possible by the increased amount of federal grants to the provincial government, which have gone up from $8 million to $45 million in Manitoba, resulting in many more millions of dollars being poured into the economy of the province. I speak of Manitoba because it is my native province. Vigorous and visionary programs of this kind constitute the reason why the present premier of Manitoba made the statement he did in the course of the last election campaign, namely that the former Conservative government had done more for the province of Manitoba than any previous administration.
Let me conclude by reminding hon. gentlemen in the government that parties are measured not by words, not by slogans, but by accomplishments. We on this side have an excellent record to present to the people of Canada in this respect. However, we make this final admonition. The nation is more important than the party, and I assure hon. gentlemen opposite that during all the deliberations of the present parliament, whether they be short or long, we on this side of the house will always place the welfare of the country above the welfare of the party. It is for this reason that the Conservative party down through the years has become identified

as the party which has done most to bring about national development and a greater sense of national unity.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I hope it will not be suggested by any hon. member that I am seeking to take away any of the rights of private members if I propose that at ten minutes before six o'clock, at the end of this debate, we do not embark upon private members' motions, which I believe would be the next item of business, but that Your Honour see it is six o'clock.
Perhaps before Your Honour looks at the clock I can say that in conformity with the announcement I made last Thursday night it would be the desire of the government to take up as a first item of business tomorrow the motion standing in the name of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister for the setting
29, 1963	441
Business of the House up of a committee on defence. Perhaps we might also have agreement, since there is agreement among all parties on this, that this motion could be amended without a formal motion to do so being made by my right hon. friend, to read "24 members" instead of "18 members" when it is taken up tomorrow.
If the debate on that motion should be concluded before the end of the day, the government would like to go ahead with the motion preceding the bill to set up the economic council of Canada. Should both these items be disposed of, the next item would be the resolution preceding the bill to set up the department of industry, and the next, the resolution respecting the Department of Agriculture.
I think that is as far as I should go, perhaps, in outlining business for tomorrow. As I announced last week, on Friday the Minister of Finance will be asking hon. members to grant to Her Majesty two months' supply both of the regular and of the supplementary estimates tabled earlier today. Once this has been disposed of-and, of course, having regard to the views expressed by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in the last parliament we would expect that to take a very few minutes-the government would then proceed in the order I suggested for tomorrow with the items of government business on Friday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the house leader has given us an outline of the business, but I think he is going to run out of items very quickly. This is the tenth day of this parliament. There are only eight items of government business on the order paper. Last year on the tenth day we had 21 items.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I can speak for the government on this, but I express the earnest hope that we will run out of that business very quickly indeed, and I invite the co-operation of hon. members on the other side of the house in running out of that business. I can assure the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that when that business is disposed of there will be plenty more to follow.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps on Friday the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings might have learned words of wisdom fiom the hon. member, now the Secretary of State, and will repeat some of the statements he made when we were dealing with interim supply.
